title: LeSTD: LLM Compression via Learning-based Sparse Tensor Decomposition
one_liner: Break the dense core tensor bottleneck in model compression by learning which core weights are truly important, then pruning the rest.
lead: Large language models have billions of weights, making them expensive to store and run. One way to shrink them is tensor decomposition: split the weight matrices into simpler pieces that take up less space. But the trick has a fatal flaw: when you split them, you create a new dense core tensor that grows huge and cancels out your savings. LeSTD fixes this by first finding a smart shared basis, then learning which pieces of the core are worth keeping and which can be thrown away.

paras: Large language models are huge: a model like GPT has 70 billion numbers (called weights) that must be stored in memory. To make them smaller, researchers use tensor decomposition, which splits each rectangular table of weights into three smaller rectangular tables that multiply back together. This works in principle: three small tables take less space than one big one.

But there is a hidden cost. When you split a 2D table of weights into three tables using decomposition, the middle table (called the core tensor) has to capture everything that does not fit into the outer tables. When you choose to use more of these 'basis' directions (essentially, more columns in the outer tables), the core grows as the square (or cube) of that number. A core that was compressed 2x can become the new bottleneck, making the whole method pointless.

callout.html: Standard tensor decomposition trades a big table of weights for a dense core tensor that grows polynomially, cancelling out the compression gain.

panels.title: 2. Decomposed into pieces
panels.caption: Split into three pieces: the core explodes if basis gets bigger.

panels.title: 3. Core tensor becomes huge
panels.caption: Core grows exponentially: the bottleneck now is what we tried to fix.

panels.title: 4. Pruning the core

panels.title: 5. Sparse core breaks through
panels.caption: Most core values are zero: storage finally drops. Accuracy is preserved.

steps.text: Run an algorithm that finds one set of basis directions that works well for all attention heads together, minimizing the information lost.
Express all attention heads in terms of this basis. The core tensor holds the coefficients that mix the basis pieces for each head.
Rank every number in the core by importance: which elements does the model rely on to keep accuracy, and which are barely used?
Delete the least important elements, replacing them with zero. The model now stores only the core's non-zero pieces.
Adjust the surviving core elements slightly (because removing a weight creates a gap, refitting fills it back in to recover lost accuracy).

object.h2: The single thing the paper changes
paras: This paper changes the core tensor: instead of a dense table full of stored values, it becomes a sparse table with mostly zeros. The basis directions stay the same; only the core is redesigned.

hidden.h2: Importance score for each core element
hidden.name: Importance score (per element)
paras: The paper measures how much each number in the core tensor contributes to the model's correct predictions. This is the 'importance': if removing a value and retraining drops accuracy a lot, that value is important. If removing it barely matters, it is unimportant.

LeSTD estimates importance by computing how sensitive the model's output is to changes in each core element. Elements with low sensitivity can be pruned away. After pruning, the remaining elements are adjusted slightly to keep predictions accurate.

heat.caption: Darker core elements are more important. Light elements can vanish without hurting accuracy.

reads.html: Imagine a checklist of building blocks in a recipe. Some ingredients (eggs, flour) make or break the dish. Others (a pinch of vanilla) barely matter. Importance is how much each ingredient changes the final flavor.
The paper uses a learned pruning score based on how sensitive the loss (error) is to each core element, or a similar sensitivity measure, to decide which elements to remove.

mechanism.h2: Why decoupling basis from sparsification works
paras: Here is what makes this approach different: the dense core problem comes from trying to do two jobs at once. Standard methods choose the basis (to capture as much information as possible) AND keep the core dense (because pruning it was not part of the design). LeSTD splits these into two separate jobs.

First, it finds the best basis without worrying about the core's size. The basis is shared across all attention heads, so it can be optimized carefully: which directions capture the most information for all heads together? This basis is usually small (rank 16 or 32), so it is efficient.

Second, it prunes the core directly. Now that the basis is fixed, the paper asks a simpler question: which core elements are actually used by the model? The core can be pruned to extreme sparsity (90%+ zeros) because the basis has already done the hard work of capturing important directions. The pruning is guided by an importance score: a measure of how much each core value affects the final predictions.

This separation works because a sparse core with a good basis can be far smaller than a dense core, even if that core has fewer basis directions. By decoupling the two jobs, LeSTD breaks the polynomial bottleneck.

Sparse decomposition: small basis, sparse core

math.h2: Reconstructing a head from basis and sparse core
math.words: Each attention head is reconstructed by multiplying the basis matrix, the sparse core matrix, and the basis matrix transposed. Only the nonzero core elements contribute to the final result.
symbols: The reconstructed weight matrix for attention head i
The shared set of basis vectors (same for all heads)
The sparse core tensor for head i (mostly zeros)
The basis transposed (multiplied on the right)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose Basis is 4×2, Core_sparse_1 is 2×2, so Basis^T is 2×4.
Original dense head matrix would be 4×4 = 16 values.
After decomposition: Basis stores 8 values, Core_sparse_1 stores 4 values but 3 are zero (1 nonzero), Basis^T stores 8 values.
Total: 8 + 1 + 8 = 17 values. But wait — Basis and Basis^T are the same storage (one shared copy), so really 8 + 1 = 9 values for this head.
If there are 8 heads and all share Basis: 8 (Basis) + 8 heads × 1 (sparse core) = 16 values vs. 8 × 16 = 128 in the dense case. Compression: 8×.
Actual LeSTD achieves much higher compression by using even sparser cores and wider bases across all MHA blocks.

math.note: The sparse core uses almost no memory because most of its entries are zero; only the nonzero entries are stored.

charts.title: Standard dense tensor decomposition
charts.note: Dense core grows with basis rank, limiting compression. Accuracy stays high but storage gain is limited.

charts.title: LeSTD with sparse core
charts.note: Sparse core is tiny; storage is halved. Accuracy stays nearly the same because important core elements are kept.

items.html: If you remove core elements that are actually important but not yet detected, accuracy will drop. The importance score must be calibrated carefully to avoid over-pruning.

items.b: Basis does not capture all heads.
items.html: If the shared basis is chosen poorly, some attention heads will be poorly represented in that basis, and pruning will hurt them more. The basis optimization step determines whether the whole method works.
After pruning, the remaining core values must be adjusted to compensate. If this step is skipped or rushed, accuracy will drop.
LeSTD works because it scores importance carefully, chooses a good basis first, and refits the core after pruning. This three-stage design avoids the pitfalls above.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small language model with 12 attention heads (like a toy GPT). Compress one multi-head attention layer using LeSTD with a rank-4 basis and target 90% core sparsity (meaning 90% of core elements become zero). Measure: (1) Storage in bytes for the original head, the dense decomposition, and the sparse decomposition. (2) Accuracy on a small test set before and after compression. (3) Time to run the finished model on both the original and compressed versions on 100 test examples.
demo.metric_eq: compression_ratio = storage_original / storage_compressed; accuracy_loss = accuracy_before - accuracy_after
demo.closing: The demo must show that LeSTD compresses 3–5x while keeping accuracy loss under 2%, and runs faster than the original because it has fewer stored numbers and can use sparse operations.
